questions.question: Which of the following best describes what happens when a class B extends class A in Java?
options: The source code of A is copied into B, so B has its own separate copy of all methods and fields defined in A.
B inherits only the public members of A; protected and package‑private members are not accessible in B.
The JVM creates a link between B and A so that B objects contain A's fields and can invoke A's methods; the code of A is not duplicated in B.
Extending A makes B a subclass that can be used anywhere an A is expected, but it does not affect the memory layout of B objects.
questions.explanation: When B extends A, Java establishes an is‑a relationship; B objects contain the instance variables declared in A (including private ones) and can call A's methods via inheritance. No source code is copied into B – the runtime uses class metadata to resolve method calls. Therefore the second option correctly describes inheritance, while the third option reflects the misconception that code is duplicated.

options: `p` is automatically treated as a `Child` at runtime, so no explicit cast is needed to access `Child` members.
`p.greet();` executes the overridden method defined in `Child`.
`p.exclusive();` can be called without a cast because the actual object is a `Child`.
`p.greet();` always invokes the version declared in `Parent` because the reference type is `Parent`.
questions.explanation: The compiler allows only methods declared in the reference type (`Parent`). At runtime, the actual object's class (`Child`) determines which overridden instance method body is executed, so `p.greet()` calls the `Child` implementation. Calls to `exclusive()` are illegal without an explicit cast because the compiler checks the reference type, not the runtime type.

questions.question: When designing a class hierarchy, which statement best captures the purpose of abstraction?
options: Abstraction requires the use of the abstract keyword on classes or methods.
Abstraction focuses on exposing essential behavior while hiding implementation details.
Abstraction is only about using interfaces to separate implementation.
Abstraction is synonymous with data hiding through private instance fields.
questions.explanation: The correct statement is that abstraction is about exposing essential behavior while hiding implementation details. The other statements incorrectly equate abstraction with data hiding or with the abstract keyword, or limit it to interfaces.

options: maxRetries is 0, debug is false, and name is null, but only after the constructor runs.
maxRetries is 0, debug is true, and name is null.
maxRetries is 0, debug is false, and name is null.
maxRetries is 0, debug is false, and name is an empty string.
questions.explanation: When an object is created, all instance fields are automatically initialized to their default values before any constructor code runs. For numeric types the default is 0, for boolean it's false, and for reference types it's null. Thus the instance created with `new Config()` has maxRetries = 0, debug = false, and name = null.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about a public top‑level class in Java is correct?
options: A public class can be declared in a file with a different name if the file contains nested classes.
A public class can be declared in a file with a different name if the file contains only package‑private classes.
A public class can be declared in any file name; the compiler will rename the file automatically.
A public class must be declared in a file whose name matches the class name, including case, before the .java extension.
questions.explanation: The statement that a public class must be declared in a file whose name matches the class name, including case, before the .java extension, is correct. The compiler requires the file name to match the public class name; otherwise a compilation error occurs. The other statements incorrectly assume the compiler will rename the file, or that a mismatch is allowed when only package‑private or nested classes are present.

options: It is automatically inherited by subclasses.
It allocates the object's memory on the heap.
It runs once during object creation to initialize instance fields.
It can be invoked on an existing object reference like a regular method.
questions.explanation: The constructor is executed only once when a new instance is created, setting up the object's state. It cannot be called on an existing object, memory allocation is handled by the new operator, and constructors are not inherited by subclasses.

questions.question: In Java, a method declared without any access modifier (default access) in class `Base` is used by a subclass `Derived` that resides in a different package. Which statement correctly describes the accessibility of that method?
options: It is visible only to classes that are in the same package as the declaring class; subclasses in other packages cannot access it.
It is accessible only within the class itself; even other classes in the same package cannot use it.
It can be accessed by subclasses regardless of their package, but not by unrelated classes in the same package.
It can be accessed by any class in any package, including subclasses, because the default modifier is equivalent to public.
questions.explanation: When no access modifier is specified, Java applies package‑private (default) access. This limits visibility to the declaring package only. Subclasses that are placed in a different package do not inherit access to such members, and the member is not public. Therefore the correct statement is that the method is visible only to classes in the same package, and subclasses in other packages cannot access it.

options: The compiler reports that the default keyword is missing.
The compiler reports that the method signature does not match any method in java.lang.Object.
The compiler reports that the interface cannot have instance fields.
The compiler reports that a default method cannot override a public method of java.lang.Object.
questions.explanation: The compiler reports that a default method cannot override a public method of java.lang.Object. The other options refer to unrelated compile errors.

options: Yes, because writing a zero-argument constructor is equivalent to the compiler-generated default constructor.
Yes, because the class has no explicit constructor.
No, because the class declares an explicit constructor.
Yes, because the compiler-generated default constructor can initialize blank final fields.
questions.explanation: The compiler only supplies a default constructor when a class declares no constructors at all. Since Example defines a constructor that takes an int, no default constructor is generated.
